related_questions.snippet: How is sepsis diagnosed? A single diagnostic test for sepsis does not yet exist, and so doctors and healthcare professionals use a combination of tests and immediate and worrisome clinical signs, which include the following: The presence of an infection. Very low blood pressure and high heart rate.

related_questions.question: How long can a person live with sepsis?

text_blocks.snippet: A person's lifespan with sepsis varies significantly depending on the severity of the infection, how quickly treatment is administered, and the individual's overall health. Some individuals with mild sepsis can recover fully with prompt treatment, while others with severe sepsis or septic shock may experience rapid decline, potentially within hours. Even with treatment, septic shock carries a high mortality rate, with up to 30-40% of cases resulting in death. Long-term survival rates vary, but many sepsis survivors face an increased risk of death in the following years, with more than half dying within five years.
snippet_highlighted_words: more than half dying within five years

list.title: Severity of Sepsis:
list.snippet: Mild sepsis may be treatable, but severe sepsis and septic shock can be fatal, sometimes within hours.

list.title: Timely Treatment:
list.snippet: Prompt diagnosis and treatment, including antibiotics and supportive care, significantly improve the chances of survival.

list.title: Individual Health:
list.snippet: Pre-existing health conditions and age can influence both short-term and long-term survival rates.

list.title: Long-Term Effects:
list.snippet: Even with successful treatment, some individuals may experience long-term complications and an increased risk of death in the following years.

list.title: Septic shock:
list.snippet: Can cause death within 12 hours if left untreated, according to medical sources.

list.title: In-hospital mortality:
list.snippet: Some studies show high in-hospital mortality rates, such as 45% in one study, and 34% within the intensive care unit (ICU), according to a study published by the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

list.title: Long-term survival:
list.snippet: Many individuals die in the months and years following sepsis, with more than half of survivors dying within five years, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

list.title: Late mortality:
list.snippet: Some research indicates that a significant number of sepsis survivors die within two years of their initial hospitalization, even if they survive the first 30 days.

list.title: Individual Variation:
list.snippet: Survival times can vary greatly depending on individual factors and the specific circumstances of the infection.

list.title: Ongoing Research:
list.snippet: Research continues to explore the underlying mechanisms of sepsis and its long-term effects on mortality.

list.title: Prompt Medical Attention:
list.snippet: Recognizing the signs and symptoms of sepsis and seeking immediate medical care is crucial for improving survival chances.

text_blocks.snippet: Sepsis diagnosis relies on identifying an infection that has triggered a dangerous overreaction of the body's immune system, leading to organ damage. There isn't a single definitive test for sepsis; diagnosis involves a combination of clinical evaluation, lab tests, and potentially imaging.
snippet_highlighted_words: relies on identifying an infection that has triggered a dangerous overreaction of the body's immune system, leading to organ damage

list.title: Clinical Assessment:
list.snippet: Doctors look for signs and symptoms like fever, chills, rapid heart rate, rapid breathing, and confusion. They also consider the patient's medical history and whether they have an existing infection.
Blood tests: Assess for signs of infection (elevated white blood cell count), clotting problems, and organ dysfunction (abnormal liver or kidney function).
Blood cultures: Identify the specific microorganism causing the infection.
Lactate measurement: May help assess the severity of sepsis and monitor treatment response.

list.title: Imaging:
list.snippet: If the source of infection is unclear, imaging tests like X-rays, CT scans, or ultrasounds may be used to identify the infection site.

list.title: SIRS Criteria:
list.snippet: The Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) criteria, involving at least two of the following, may be used to identify potential sepsis:
Temperature above 100.4°F (38°C) or below 96.8°F (36°C).
Heart rate above 90 beats per minute.
Respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute or PaCO2 less than 32 mm Hg.
White blood cell count above 12,000 per μL or below 4,000 per μL, or greater than 10% immature forms.

list.title: qSOFA Score:
list.snippet: The quick SOFA (qSOFA) score is a bedside tool that can be used to assess the risk of sepsis. It includes:
Altered mental status.
Systolic blood pressure of 100 mmHg or less.
Respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute or higher.
A score of 2 or more suggests a higher risk of sepsis.

list.title: SOFA Score:
list.snippet: The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score is used in the ICU to assess organ dysfunction.

list.title: Specialized Tests:
list.snippet: In some cases, tests like pulse oximetry (to measure blood oxygen saturation) or tests to check for meningitis (lumbar puncture, CT, or MRI) may be used.
Sepsis can progress rapidly, so early diagnosis and treatment are crucial.
There is no single test to definitively diagnose sepsis, and providers rely on a combination of factors.
The qSOFA and SOFA scores are helpful but have limitations and should not be used as the sole criteria for diagnosis, according to the American Academy of Family Physicians.
Sepsis is not contagious, but the infections that can cause it are.
